Neonates of the Ocellate spot skate emerge from their egg cases at a total length of 5.5 centimeters [Lb = 5.5 centimeters], a value derived from scaling relationships observed in the related little skate Leucoraja erinacea, in which a 9.7-centimeter total length at birth corresponds to a 32.4-centimeter ultimate disk width. This dimensional comparison suggests that the newborn skate is proportionally quite small relative to its potential adult size, a trait consistent with an altricial developmental strategy common among many rajiform elasmobranchs. Upon emergence, the yolk sac is fully resorbed, and the pup must commence independent foraging almost immediately, targeting small benthic crustaceans and polychaetes in the shallow coastal waters of its Northwest Pacific range. The relatively modest size at birth likely influences early juvenile survival, as these tiny individuals face considerable predation pressure from larger demersal fishes and cephalopods before reaching a size refuge.

As females approach the completion of their somatic growth trajectory, the ultimate disk width attained by adults is estimated at approximately 57 centimeters [Li = approximately 57 centimeters], a measurement that places Okamejei kenojei among the medium-sized skates within the Rajidae family. This asymptotic dimension is reached only after several years of sustained growth, during which the animal transitions through juvenile and sub-adult stages. The disk width itself serves as a reliable predictor of reproductive potential, given that larger females are capable of accommodating a greater number of developing eggs within their oviducal glands. Comparative studies among congeneric species indicate that this ultimate size is consistent with a life history strategy that prioritizes moderate fecundity over rapid turnover, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by the production of large, well-yolked egg cases.

The onset of sexual maturation in Ocellate spot skate is marked by the attainment of a disk width of 39 centimeters [Lp = 39 centimeters], at which point females begin to exhibit ovarian development and males display elongation of the claspers. This pubertal threshold represents a critical juncture in the life history, as it signals the shift from an energy allocation strategy focused predominantly on somatic growth toward one that incorporates reproductive investment. Field surveys have documented that individuals reaching this size are typically between three and four years of age, although local environmental conditions, particularly water temperature and food availability, can modulate the precise timing of maturation. The 39-centimeter disk width at puberty therefore provides a useful morphological criterion for assessing population-level maturity schedules and for informing fisheries management measures aimed at protecting pre-reproductive juveniles.

Under controlled experimental conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], captive females have been observed to achieve a maximum reproductive rate of 150 eggs per year [Ri = 150 eggs per year], a value derived from continuous monitoring of oviposition events over multiple breeding cycles. This elevated output, sustained across the warmer months, reflects the species' capacity for nearly year-round egg production when thermal conditions are favorable and prey resources remain abundant. The 22 °C regime is representative of the peak summer temperatures encountered in the shallow demersal habitats of the Yellow Sea and the East China Sea, where the species is most commonly collected. At this temperature, the interval between successive ovipositions is relatively compressed, allowing a single gravid female to deposit up to three or four egg cases per week during the height of the reproductive season.

Longevity records for Ocellate spot skate, gathered from both captive holding facilities and mark-recapture field studies conducted at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], indicate that the species can persist for approximately 13.3 years [am = approximately 13.3 years], a lifespan that is notably extended relative to many other small-bodied rajids. This prolonged existence, measured from hatching to natural senescence, is consistent with a slow life-history pace characterized by delayed maturation, modest annual fecundity, and a relatively high investment per offspring. The physiological mechanisms underlying this extended longevity likely include low basal metabolic rates and efficient antioxidant defense systems, traits that are common among elasmobranchs and that contribute to their generally slow rates of aging. At 22 °C, somatic death typically follows a gradual decline in feeding activity and body condition, marking the completion of a life cycle that integrates all the aforementioned growth and reproductive milestones.
